extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in humour, culture, and media
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic summary of the genre 'toilet humour' describing its subject matter, typical audiences, forms (music, performance, books, games, toys), cultural functions (taboo rejection, satire) and examples. Useful for understanding how and where toilet humour appears and is received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter (bodily functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Toilet humour is a type of off-colour humour dealing with: defecation (including diarrhea and constipation), urination, flatulence, or, to a lesser extent, vomiting and other bodily functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defines the permissible topical scope for toilet humour; pieces that center on these bodily functions fall into the category. Examples in the article include scatological humour (defecation) and flatulence humour (flatulence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific sublabels are used: 'scatological humour' for defecation and 'flatulence humor' for flatulence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the precise term that matches the bodily function emphasized (e.g., scatology for feces-related humour). The page provides these label distinctions as part of categorizing works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical audience and developmental appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Toilet humour is commonly an interest of toddlers and young children, for whom cultural taboos related to acknowledgement of waste excretion still have a degree of novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating toilet humour, consider age: material that exploits novelty/taboo often appeals to young children; suitability for adult vs child audiences should be assessed accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of comedic effect — taboo rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: The humour comes from the rejection of such taboos, and is a part of modern culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective toilet humour often relies on violating cultural taboos about waste and bodily functions; evaluating effectiveness should consider how the work frames or subverts those taboos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use in music and songs
rubrics_metrics.description: Toilet humour is sometimes found in song and rhyme, particularly schoolboy songs; historical and contemporary musical examples appear (e.g., Mozart and scatology; the Scheiße-Lied; Enrique y Ana's 'Caca Culo Pedo Pis'; Eminem lines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing musical humour, look for scatological lyrics, parody songs, or recurring motifs in folk/school songs and popular music. Reception may vary from nostalgic/folk contexts to critical backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance and stage acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage performances use toilet humour physically and visually (examples: Mr. Methane farting musical notes; Le Pétomane; comedy sketches by Tim & Eric featuring fake commercials for grotesque products).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate performance works for inventive physical gags, prop design, shock value and theatricality; examples show both historic novelty acts and modern sketch-comedy approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controversy and critical reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Toilet humour can provoke criticism or lament from reviewers and parents (example: Eminem lyric 'Your booty is heavy duty, like diarrhea' received extensive lament; Los Angeles Times remark labeling it 'a parent's nightmare').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should consider likely critical response and parental/guardian concerns; controversial lines or imagery may yield strong negative reactions even if appreciated by some audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical and political use
rubrics_metrics.description: Toilet humour can be used as satire to criticize social or political conditions (example: Vladimir Voinovich used toilet humour to criticize Soviet food policies in novels like Moscow 2042).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When used satirically, scatological imagery is a rhetorical device to portray corruption, degradation or to invert official narratives; evaluate whether the bodily-function imagery advances the satire's argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use in children's literature and character naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Children's series (e.g., Captain Underpants) make copious use of toilet humor in character names and plots (e.g., 'Doctor Diaper', 'Professor Pippy Pee-Pee Poopypants').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For children’s media, consider whether toilet-based names and gags serve playful potty-training-friendly humor or rely on lowbrow shock; evaluate appropriateness for intended age-group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration into video game design and mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: Video games sometimes incorporate scatological jokes and mechanics (examples: Conker's Bad Fur Day's 'Poo Mountain' and boss 'The Great Mighty Poo'; Metal Gear series' toilet/urination gags; Death Stranding allowing urination/defecation with gameplay effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging games, look at how toilet humour is embedded: as environmental jokes, combat mechanics, character moves, or item systems; assess whether it enhances gameplay, worldbuilding or is gratuitous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toy design and educational/potty-training function
rubrics_metrics.description: Toys often simulate urination/defecation (e.g., Little Live 'Gotta Go' Pets that 'poop', Barbie's dog Tanner, infant dolls that pee/poop). Parenting blogs praised some lines for potty training; critics call others 'disgusting' or inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate such toys on design intent (potty-training utility vs gross-out novelty), safety/age-appropriateness, and likely parental reception; balance educational claims against criticisms of immaturity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre labels and related themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Toilet humour is associated with related genres/themes such as 'sophomoric humour', 'gross out', 'grotesque body', 'flatulence humour', and 'dick joke'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify works by their overlap with these broader categories; this helps set expectations for tone, sophistication, and target audience when producing or evaluating material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural and historical contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Toilet humour appears across history and cultures (examples include historical woodcuts, folk songs, and literary satire); cultural position influences acceptability and form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments should take local cultural norms and historical precedents into account—what is taboo or humorous in one context may differ in another. The article cites historical examples (Papstspotbilder, folk songs) to illustrate continuity.
